column1: # What MRK-1, the defaults reference, shows for each key in
# config/defaults.tsv. The page reads this file when it loads, and other
# programs can read it too. check-defaults-desc fails, and so make check fails,
# when a key there has no line here, when a line here has no key there, or when
# a line is not one description.
# One description on each line: nine fields, separated by tabs.
#   domain       the defaults domain, as config/defaults.tsv has it
#   key          the key, as config/defaults.tsv has it
#   title        the name of the setting
#   category     a word that groups the settings, such as Security or Finder
#   default      the value macOS has when nothing sets the key, or empty
#   preference   true for a personal choice that may not suit everyone, else
#   description  what the key does now
#   why          why mrk sets it, or empty
#   background   history and other notes that are not Simplified Technical
# The domain, key, title, category, preference and description are never
# empty. Each field is plain text, not HTML. In a field, a backslash starts an
# escape: \t is a tab, \n is a newline and \\ is a backslash. A line that
# starts with # is a comment, and an empty line is ignored. Two lines with the
# same domain and key are refused.
# The same key, type and value in two domains of one section of
# config/defaults.tsv is one setting. It has one line here, for the first of
# the domains. The trackpad keys are like this.
# The lines are in the order of config/defaults.tsv. Add a new line at the

column7: Turns on Dark Mode for the whole system. It changes the menu bar, the Dock, the window frames and most built-in apps. The key accepts only the string "Dark". There is no "Light" value, so you delete the key to go back to Light Mode: defaults delete NSGlobalDomain AppleInterfaceStyle.
column9: macOS 10.14 Mojave introduced Dark Mode in 2018. A partial dark menu bar existed from Yosemite (10.10), but it used a different mechanism.

column7: Sets when macOS shows the scrollbars. "Always" keeps them visible. "Automatic" lets macOS decide from the input device: hidden for a trackpad, visible for a mouse. "WhenScrolling" hides them until you scroll. "Always" overrides the automatic device detection.
column8: Overlay scrollbars appear and disappear dynamically, shifting layout and moving click targets. Always-visible scrollbars provide a consistent, predictable interface.
column9: Scrollbars were always visible before OS X 10.7 Lion, which ported the iOS overlay-scrollbar paradigm to the Mac.

column7: Makes Finder show the file extension for every file. This includes the types that macOS hides by default, such as .jpg, .txt and .mov. A single file can still override this with its own "Hide extension" attribute.
column8: Hidden extensions can make malicious files appear harmless — a macOS app bundle named "invoice.pdf.app" displays as "invoice.pdf" with extensions hidden.
column9: This setting is also CIS Benchmark control 6.2 for macOS hardening.

column7: Turns off the scale-up animation that plays when a window first appears, so a window opens at once. It applies only to the apps that you start after you apply it. Start a running app again for the change to reach it. The compositor handles some animations in newer macOS, and this key does not change those.
column8: Eliminates visual delay when rapidly switching or tiling windows.
column9: OS X 10.7 Lion introduced this key.

column7: Sets the speed of the sheet animation, not the window resize speed that the key name suggests. A sheet is a dialog that rolls down from the title bar of a window, such as Save or Print. The default is 0.2 seconds. A value of 0.001 makes a dialog appear almost at once.
column8: The default 0.2s delay is perceptible and compounds across dozens of daily Save/Print interactions.
column9: Despite its name, this key does not affect general window resizing, and many dotfiles misidentify it as a window-resize setting. Robservatory.com measured a 47% time reduction for repeated Save dialog workflows.

column7: Turns off Resume. Resume restores all the windows from your last session when you start an app again. A value of false matches "Close windows when quitting an app" in System Settings → Desktop & Dock.
column8: Stale windows from a previous session can cause confusion after crashes or updates — apps reopen to whatever state they were in, which is rarely useful.
column9: Resume arrived in OS X 10.7 Lion and was immediately controversial; "how do I disable Resume?" was among the most-searched Lion questions in 2011. Apple finally surfaced it as a visible toggle in Ventura.

column7: Makes a Save dialog open in expanded mode, which shows the full directory browser. Set this key together with its "2" variant. The second key covers the other Save panel contexts that document-scoped saving added.
column8: The collapsed panel hides the destination path. Files frequently end up saved to the wrong location because the user accepted a default they couldn't see.
column9: Apple introduced the simplified collapsed Save dialog in OS X 10.7 Lion. Before that, Save dialogs always showed the full hierarchy.

column7: Works with NSNavPanelExpandedStateForSaveMode. It covers the other document-saving contexts, which use a separate code path. Set both keys together, so all apps behave the same way.
Makes a Print dialog open fully expanded. The expanded dialog shows the paper size, the orientation, the quality and the other options at once. Set this key together with its "2" variant.
column9: The simplified collapsed Print dialog arrived in OS X 10.7 Lion alongside the collapsed Save dialog, and was equally unpopular.

column7: Works with PMPrintingExpandedStateForPrint. It covers the other print dialog contexts. Set both keys together, so all apps behave the same way.

column3: Default New Documents to Local Storage
column7: Stops the iCloud-aware apps from using iCloud Drive as the default location for a new document. These apps include TextEdit, Pages, Preview, Numbers and Keynote. A value of false keeps local storage as the default. You can still save to iCloud by hand.
column8: Avoids accidental sync of sensitive or work-in-progress files to iCloud without explicit intent.
column9: Apple introduced iCloud document storage in OS X Mountain Lion (10.8, 2012) and set it as the default save location — a decision that surprised many users who later found their documents "missing" (stored in iCloud, not locally).

column7: Sets the speed of the Quick Look panel animation. A value of 0 stops the animation, but only for the close (zoom-out) step. The open (zoom-in) animation does not change.
column9: Quick Look debuted in Mac OS X 10.5 Leopard (2007). The close-only behaviour dates from El Capitan (10.11); community reports from 2016 confirmed it is intentional, not a bug.

column7: A double-click on a window title bar minimises the window. The other accepted value is "Maximize", which zooms the window instead.
column8: Zoom is already on the green button. Minimise is the action with no other one-step control.

column7: Sets the tint behind selected text and selected items. The value is three space-separated floats: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 1.
Sets the icon size in the sidebar of Finder, Mail and System Settings. 1 is small, 2 is medium, 3 is large.
Turns off the two-finger horizontal swipe that moves back and forward through pages.
column8: A sideways scroll inside a wide table or a code view otherwise navigates away and discards the half-completed form.

column7: Turns off Force Click and its haptic feedback. A firm press then does nothing extra.
Sets the longest gap, in seconds, that still counts as a double-click. A larger number gives you more time between the two clicks.

Sets the system alert volume. A value of 0 makes the alert silent. The key changes only the alert audio channel: the error sounds, the notification chimes and the volume-limit feedback. It does not change media playback in an app such as Spotify or Safari. Core Audio routes the alert channel separately from the main output volume.

Turns off the interface sound effects. These include the drag-to-trash swoosh, the empty-trash rumble and the other interaction sounds. A value of 0 matches "Play user interface sound effects" turned off in System Settings → Sound.
Sets which system sound plays for an alert. The value is a full path to an audio file in /System/Library/Sounds.

Sets the interval between repeated characters when you hold a key. The unit is about 16.7 ms, so a value of 2 gives about 33 ms. The System Settings slider covers a limited range, and defaults write accepts a value below that minimum. A value of 1 is faster than System Settings can set. Log out and log in again for the change to take effect.

Do not set a value below 10, which is about 167 ms: a delay that short repeats characters by accident. This key sets the delay before key repeat starts when you hold a key. The unit is about 16.7 ms, so a value of 15 gives about 250 ms. That is shorter than the System Settings minimum of 25, which is about 420 ms. Log out and log in again for the change to take effect.

column3: Disable Accent Picker, Restore Key Repeat
column7: Turns off the accent-character picker that appears when you hold a key, and restores the traditional key repeat. macOS gives no System Settings toggle for this key. Use defaults write, or a third-party tool such as TinkerTool.
column8: The accent picker interrupts keyboard-driven navigation and editing. Holding j or k in a text editor should repeat the character, not open a popup.
column9: The popup arrived in OS X 10.7 Lion as a direct port of iOS keyboard behavior, replacing decades of key-repeat defaults. It was one of the first popular Lion customization tips — osxdaily.com covered it within days of Lion's July 2011 release — and as of 2024 Apple still provides no System Settings toggle.

column7: Turns on full keyboard navigation, so Tab moves the focus to every control. This includes the buttons, the checkboxes and the radio buttons, not only the text fields and the lists. A value of 2 turns it on, and values 2 and 3 behave the same way on current macOS. The System Settings toggle is Keyboard → "Keyboard navigation". Press Control-F7 to toggle it without a settings change.
column8: Allows Tab to cycle through all controls — buttons, radio buttons, checkboxes — without reaching for the mouse.

column7: Turns off the automatic capitalization of the first word after a period. It matches "Capitalize words automatically" turned off in System Settings → Keyboard → Text Replacements.
column8: Breaks commands, code, and domain names entered in text fields outside terminals.
column9: This key belongs to the NSAutomatic* family of text-correction features, ported from iOS keyboard intelligence to macOS.

column7: Turns off the automatic dash substitution. macOS otherwise replaces two hyphens with an en dash (–), and three hyphens with an em dash (—).
column8: Silently converts "--" to an em dash, breaking markdown, CLI flags, and code pasted into apps with smart dashes enabled.

column7: Turns off the double-space substitution. macOS otherwise inserts a period and a space when you type two spaces.
column8: Interferes with intentional double-spacing in code, indentation, and command entry.
column9: The gesture is a port of the iOS keyboard behavior.

column7: Turns off the smart-quote substitution. macOS otherwise replaces the straight apostrophes and quotation marks with curly typographic ones.
column8: Curly quotes break shell scripts, JSON, code snippets, and command-line arguments. The substitution is invisible until something fails.

column7: Turns off the automatic spelling correction. It matches "Correct spelling automatically" turned off in System Settings → Keyboard → Text Replacements.
column8: Mangles technical terms, hostnames, variable names, and other domain-specific vocabulary that the system dictionary doesn't recognize.

column7: Turns off automatic spelling correction inside WebKit text fields. This covers Safari and any app that shows web content.
column8: This is a separate key from NSAutomaticSpellingCorrectionEnabled. Set only that one and Safari still corrects your typing.

column7: Sets what the globe key does. 0 is nothing, 1 changes the input source, 2 shows the emoji picker and 3 starts dictation.
column8: Dictation is off on this Mac, so the key would otherwise open a feature that is disabled.

column7: Sets the position of the Dock on the screen. The values are "left", "bottom" and "right". Run killall Dock for the change to take effect. With more than one display, the Dock appears on the display that System Settings → Displays → Arrangement makes primary.

Sets the size of the Dock icons in pixels. The range is about 16 to 128. The System Settings slider starts near 36 to 48, which depends on the display resolution. Run killall Dock for the change to take effect.
Sets the window minimize animation. "genie" uses the stretchy drain-into-Dock effect. "scale" shrinks the window in place. A third value, "suck", also works, but it never appears in System Settings.
column9: The "suck" value is a vacuum-like animation. It has existed since macOS 10.0, reportedly even in pre-release builds, but has never appeared in System Preferences; the popular theory is that Apple kept it hidden because of the name. All three values work on macOS 15.

column5: false (minimized windows appear as separate thumbnails)
column7: Makes a minimized window shrink into the Dock icon of its app. The window does not become a separate thumbnail in the minimized-windows area of the Dock.
column8: Minimized windows otherwise accumulate as separate thumbnails in the Dock, cluttering it. This keeps the Dock layout stable regardless of how many windows are minimized.

column7: Turns off both kinds of Dock icon bounce. These are the launch bounce, which plays while an app starts, and the alert bounce, which plays when an app wants your attention.
column8: Eliminates attention-hijacking animations during focused work. If an app needs attention, the notification will still appear — it just won't be accompanied by a bouncing icon.
column9: In macOS 10.3 Panther these were two separate keys: launchanim controlled the launch bounce and had a UI checkbox in Dock preferences, while no-bouncing controlled the notification bounce. Both remain independently settable today.

column7: Hides the "Recent Applications" section of the Dock. A divider separates this section, and it shows the apps that you used recently but did not pin.
column9: macOS 10.14 Mojave introduced this section in 2018 and turns it on by default. Power users with curated Dock layouts typically disable it.

column7: Sets the delay before a hidden Dock appears again when the cursor reaches the screen edge. The default is about 0.5 seconds, and a value of 0 shows the Dock at once. The delay is visible only when Dock auto-hide is on. This script does not turn auto-hide on, but the value applies if you turn it on later.

Turns off the Finder animations. These include the Get Info window, the icon movement and the scroll overscroll bounce. Run killall Finder for the change to take effect. Some animations in newer macOS use compositor layers, and this key does not change those.
column8: Makes file operations feel instant. Each animation adds visible latency per action, which compounds across a day of file management.
column9: This is one of the earliest macOS performance tips, documented since about 2007.

column7: Shows the path bar along the bottom of a Finder window. The bar gives the folder chain, and each part of it accepts a drop.
Shows the status bar along the bottom of a Finder window. It reports the item count and the free space on the disk.
Puts the full POSIX path of the current folder in the Finder window title, instead of the folder name alone.
column8: The title is then something you can read a path out of and paste into a terminal.

column7: Keeps folders above files when a Finder window sorts by name.
Sets the view a new Finder window opens in. "Nlsv" is list, "icnv" is icon, "clmv" is column and "glyv" is gallery.
Sets where a Finder search starts. "SCcf" searches the current folder, "SCev" searches the whole Mac and "SCsp" searches the previous scope.
column8: A search that starts at the whole Mac returns thousands of results when you meant the folder in front of you.

column7: Turns off the confirmation that appears when you change a file extension.
column8: The dialog fires on every rename that touches the extension, which teaches you to dismiss it without reading.

column7: Turns off the confirmation that appears when you empty the Trash.
Sets the folder a new Finder window opens. "PfDe" is the Desktop, "PfHm" is the home folder and "PfAF" is Recents.
column8: A target other than these three also needs NewWindowTargetPath, which holds an absolute path and does not move between machines.

column7: Shows the internal hard disks on the Desktop.
Keeps connected network servers off the Desktop.
Adds a Quit item to the Finder menu, so Cmd-Q closes Finder. Finder restarts when you next open a window.
Opens a folder in a new window rather than a new tab.

Turns off the drop shadow that macOS adds to a window screenshot, which you take with Cmd+Shift+4 and then Space. A value of true gives a clean PNG file with no shadow padding. The key changes the window captures only. A region capture and a full-screen capture never have a shadow. Run killall SystemUIServer for the change to take effect.
column8: Shadows add invisible padding around the image canvas and visual noise in documentation, where a clean window edge is more useful than a soft drop shadow.
column9: The shadow adds transparent padding around the image, and it was a celebrated feature of Mac screenshots from the Leopard era.

column7: On macOS 15 Sequoia this preference may not persist, because it can reset itself without warning. The key hides the floating thumbnail preview that appears after you take a screenshot.
column8: The thumbnail overlays the screen for several seconds after each capture and delays access to the file path — it adds friction without adding information.
column9: macOS 10.14 Mojave introduced the thumbnail. Multiple reports, including MacRumors forum threads specific to 15.3.2, confirm the setting spontaneously resets itself on Sequoia, sometimes multiple times per day.

column7: Sets whether the capture date and time appear in the screenshot filename. A value of true gives a name such as "Screenshot 2025-03-20 at 13.27.20.png". A value of false gives "Screenshot.png", and adds a number to each later capture. Run killall SystemUIServer for the change to take effect.
column8: Predictable, date-free filenames are easier to reference in scripts, automation, and documentation without needing to know the exact capture time.

column7: Sets the default save location for every screenshot. Make sure that the directory exists: if it is absent, a screenshot can fail without a message. Run killall SystemUIServer for the change to take effect.
column9: Before macOS 10.14 Mojave you could change this only with defaults write, because no UI option existed. Mojave added the location picker to the Shift-Cmd-5 screenshot toolbar.

column7: Draws a circle at each mouse click in a screen recording.
column8: A recording of a workflow is hard to follow when the clicks are invisible.

column7: Stops Finder from creating .DS_Store and ._ (AppleDouble) sidecar files on a network volume. This covers AFP, SMB, NFS and WebDAV. A .DS_Store file stores the view preferences of a directory, and on a network share it can also slow SMB browsing. The key does not delete the .DS_Store files that already exist.
column8: .DS_Store files expose directory metadata and appear as visible clutter to Windows and Linux users on shared volumes.
column9: Apple has an official support article (HT208209) recommending this setting for enterprise SMB environments.

column7: Stops macOS from writing .DS_Store and ._ (AppleDouble) sidecar files to a USB drive, an SD card and other removable media.
column8: Portable drives are frequently shared across OSes. .DS_Store files are invisible on macOS but show up as junk on Windows and Linux.

column7: Skips the checksum check when macOS mounts a disk image (.dmg) file. This key is probably not effective on current macOS: DiskImageMounter appears to ignore it, but it writes without an error. The checksum check finds corruption and tampering, so skipping it for a downloaded image is a security trade-off.
column8: Verification is redundant when the source is trusted and skips multi-second delays on large installers. Note: likely a no-op since El Capitan.
column9: Community reports indicate DiskImageMounter has ignored these keys since OS X 10.11.3 El Capitan, although they still write without an error.

column7: Skips the checksum check for a locked disk image. Like skip-verify, this key is probably not effective on current macOS.
Skips the "Verifying..." spinner for a disk image that you downloaded from the internet. Like the other two verify keys, this key is probably not effective on current macOS.
column9: Of the three verify keys, this one was historically the most visible to the user.

column3: Suppress Time Machine New Disk Prompt
column7: Stops the "Do you want to use [disk] to back up with Time Machine?" dialog that appears when you connect a blank external drive. The key hides the prompt only. It does not turn Time Machine off, and it does not change an existing backup destination. Clicking "Don't Use" normally writes an invisible .com.apple.timemachine.donotpresent marker file to that one volume. This key instead hides the prompt for every new disk.
column8: Prevents Time Machine dialogs from interrupting when external drives are connected for other purposes — archiving, file transfers, etc.

column7: Sets what the Activity Monitor Dock icon shows while the app runs. The values are 0 for the standard icon, 2 for the network usage and 3 for the disk usage. Value 5 gives the CPU meter bar, and value 6 gives the CPU history graph. This script uses 2, which shows mirrored network line graphs.
column8: Makes system activity visible at a glance in the Dock without needing to switch windows.
column9: Most dotfiles use 5, the CPU meter, for at-a-glance load visibility.

column7: Sets the default process filter. Value 100 shows All Processes. The other values are 101 for My Processes, 102 for System Processes and 103 for Other Processes. Value 106 shows Active Processes, and value 107 shows Windowed Processes.
column8: The default "My Processes" view hides background and system processes that may be consuming significant resources.

column7: Sets the default sort column. CPUUsage sorts by CPU consumption, which puts a runaway process at the top. The other values include CPUTime, PID, ProcessName, RealPrivateMemory and PhysicalMemory.
column8: Surfaces the highest-load process immediately on open, without manually clicking a column header each time.

column7: Sets the sort direction. Value 0 sorts descending, which puts the highest values first, and value 1 sorts ascending. Value 0 with CPUUsage puts the most CPU-hungry processes at the top.

Sets the refresh interval of Activity Monitor in seconds. Value 1 refreshes every second and is the most responsive. Value 2 refreshes every 2 seconds, and value 5 every 5 seconds. A more frequent refresh adds a small amount of CPU overhead from the monitoring process.
column8: The 5s default misses short-lived CPU spikes. A runaway process can max out a core and settle down before the display refreshes.

column7: Makes a new TextEdit document open as plain text (.txt) instead of rich text (.rtf).
column8: RTF creates binary files that can't be read by other editors, diffed in git, or inspected as plain text. TextEdit is most useful as a scratch-pad for plain text.
column9: The default RTF mode has confused many users who expected a plain text editor — pasting code into an RTF document silently corrupts formatting with invisible markup. This is one of the most commonly cited macOS developer setup tips, and it has existed as a preference since early Mac OS X.

column7: Sets the profile that Terminal uses for a new window. "Pro" is a built-in profile with a dark background and light text. This key holds the profile name as a string, so the name must match a profile that Terminal has.
column9: The key name contains spaces, which is unusual for a defaults key. Quote it on the command line, or the shell splits it into three arguments.

column7: Sets the profile that Terminal uses for the window it opens at startup. Set this key together with "Default Window Settings". If you set only one of the two, the first window does not match the windows that you open later.

Take care with this key: if the cursor drifts over a Terminal window while you type elsewhere, that window takes the input. The key turns on X11-style focus-follows-mouse for Terminal. A Terminal window under the cursor accepts keyboard input without a click. macOS does not raise the window, so the focus moves silently.
column8: Avoids needing to click to focus a terminal window when working across multiple panes, reducing hand movement.

column7: Stops other processes from reading the keystrokes that you type into Terminal. These processes include the screen readers, the accessibility tools, TextExpander and a possible keylogger. The trade-off is that TextExpander and similar keyboard-monitoring utilities stop working in a Terminal window.
column8: Prevents other processes from intercepting keystrokes typed into Terminal — including passwords, private keys, and API tokens.
column9: This is a Level 1 recommendation in the CIS Apple macOS benchmarks — control 6.4.1 in the Ventura benchmark, with equivalents in earlier versions.

column7: Turns off the line mark gutter. The gutter shows a small arrow in the left margin of Terminal, at the start of each shell prompt. The arrows help you move between command outputs. A value of false hides them.
Sets the directory a new Terminal tab opens in. 1 is the default working directory rather than the directory of the current tab.

Run killall ControlCenter for a clock change to take effect. killall SystemUIServer does not work for the clock keys, and the wrong process leaves no visible change. This key sets the menu bar clock to digital with false, or to an analog circular face with true.
column9: The clock keys moved to ControlCenter in macOS Big Sur (11.0). Before that, killall SystemUIServer applied them.

column7: Shows the AM/PM designator in the menu bar clock for 12-hour time. Run killall ControlCenter for the change to take effect, not killall SystemUIServer.
Shows the abbreviated day of the week, such as "Thu", in the menu bar clock. Run killall ControlCenter for the change to take effect, not killall SystemUIServer.

column3: Show Date in Menu Bar Clock
column7: Sets when the menu bar clock shows the date. Value 0 never shows it, value 1 always shows it, and value 2 shows it when space allows. Run killall ControlCenter for the change to take effect, not killall SystemUIServer.
column9: macOS 12.4 Monterey introduced this key to replace the older boolean ShowDayOfMonth key, which had no "when space allows" middle option. A dotfile that still sets ShowDayOfMonth uses the deprecated predecessor.

column7: Flashes the colon between the hours and the minutes once a second.

column5: false on a desktop trackpad; true on many notebooks after Setup Assistant
column7: Turns off tap-to-click. You must press the trackpad until it clicks. A tap alone does nothing.
column8: A resting finger can register a tap and move the cursor or select text by accident.

column7: Turns off Force Touch. A hard press no longer triggers a force click, and it no longer gives haptic feedback for that gesture.
column8: A force click fires on a firm ordinary click and opens a lookup panel that interrupts the task.
column9: Apple added Force Touch to the trackpad with the Retina MacBook in 2015. The trackpad does not move; a Taptic Engine simulates the click.

column7: Turns off the haptic detent the trackpad fires on a click. The click still registers, without the tap you feel.

column3: Secondary Click in the Bottom-Right Corner
column7: Sets the secondary click to the bottom-right corner of the trackpad. Value 2 selects the bottom-right corner. Value 1 selects the bottom-left corner. Value 0 turns the corner click off.
Turns off the five-finger pinch that opens Launchpad.
Turns off the four-finger horizontal swipe that moves between full-screen apps and Spaces.
Turns off the four-finger pinch that opens Launchpad, and the four-finger spread that shows the desktop.
Turns off the four-finger vertical swipe that opens Mission Control.
Turns off the two-finger pinch that zooms in and out.
column8: The pinch fires during ordinary two-finger scrolling and changes the zoom level without intent.

column7: Turns off the two-finger secondary click. Use the bottom-right corner instead. See TrackpadCornerSecondaryClick.
Turns off the two-finger rotate gesture.
column8: The rotate gesture can turn an image or a PDF page by accident during a two-finger scroll.

column7: Turns off three-finger drag. You cannot move a window with three fingers.
column9: macOS Sierra moved this control out of the Trackpad pane and into Accessibility → Pointer Control → Trackpad Options. The defaults key still works.

column7: Turns off the three-finger horizontal swipe that moves between full-screen apps and Spaces.
Turns off the three-finger tap that looks up a word or shows data detectors. Value 0 turns the gesture off. Value 2 turns it on.
Turns off the three-finger vertical swipe that opens Mission Control and App Expose.
Turns off the two-finger double tap that zooms into a page or an image.
Turns off the two-finger swipe from the right edge that opens Notification Centre.
column8: The gesture fires when you scroll near the right edge, and the panel covers the window.

column7: Sets how a secondary click is made on a trackpad. 1 is a click in the bottom-right corner.
column8: This is the global half of the setting. The two trackpad domains carry TrackpadCornerSecondaryClick, and the corner click does not work unless both are set.

column7: Turns off personalised advertising in the App Store, Apple News and Stocks.
Stops Apple's advertising platform from using the advertising identifier to target you.
Stops the crash reporter dialog from appearing. "none" hides it, "basic" shows it and "developer" adds the full report.
column8: A background process that crashes should not put a dialog in front of you for a report you do not send.

column7: Stops a click on the wallpaper from hiding every window to reveal the Desktop.
column8: macOS Sonoma turned this on by default. A stray click near the edge of the screen then clears the screen.

column7: Sets how Stage Manager groups windows. 1 shows one window at a time, 0 groups every window of an application.
Turns Siri off. The Ask Siri feature stops, and macOS does not send a request to Apple's servers.
Stops the Mac from listening for the Siri wake word. Wake-word detection keeps the microphone active at all times.
column8: Every other route into Siri on this Mac is already closed. The wake word was the one part still running for a feature that is never used.

column7: Stops the voice-trigger daemon from listening for the wake word.
column8: This is a second wake-word switch, in its own domain. Turning off the one in com.apple.Siri leaves this at true, and the detector keeps running.

column7: Removes the Siri icon from the menu bar.
Turns off Siri Suggestions in Spotlight, Safari and the Look Up panel.
Turns Dictation off. macOS then does not offer to transcribe speech into a text field, and it does not download the on-device speech model.
column8: The prompt that appears when you press the globe key turns Dictation on with one click, which is how it came to be enabled here. The speech model is close to a gigabyte, and nothing on this Mac had used it since 2024.

column7: Records the answer to "Improve Siri & Dictation". 0 means the question was never put, 1 opts in and 2 opts out.
column8: The value is an explicit answer rather than a default, so 2 is a decision and 0 is only an unanswered prompt.

column7: Lets a shortcut key speak the text you have selected.
The newer mirror of the Speak Selection switch, in the Accessibility domain. Set both, or the two panes disagree.
Copies only the address when you copy a name from a message header. Mail otherwise copies the display name and the address together.
column8: Pasting a name and an address into a terminal or a web form is almost never the intent.

column5: The first calendar in the list
column7: Puts a new event in the calendar you last selected. The alternative value is the identifier of one specific calendar.
column8: A calendar identifier is different on each machine, so the sentinel is the only value that travels.

column7: Limits AirDrop to your contacts. The accepted values are "Everyone", "Contacts Only" and "Off".
column8: With "Everyone", any device in range can raise a transfer prompt on this Mac. That is the setting unsolicited AirDrop relies on.
